catalog_quote: p.155: "22.5 Word stress. The word stress on two-syllable words in Wai Wai normally occurs on the last syllable of the word. ... But if such words are followed by certain particles ( I am not sure if the rule holds for all particles or not) ... nouns or adverbs having three syllables and having a CV pattern stress normally occurs on the last syllable. If they have four syllables, the stress falls on the penultimate syllable. In either case stress falls on the syllable following the syllable having the long vowel. (717) o-ko-'mo 'wasp' (718) ta-ma-'ta-ma 'butterfly' (719) o-co-'ro 'hot' (720) xa-ma-'pe 'pale' (721) pu-ru-'pu-rpe 'floating' ... verbs and in words derived from verb stems the stress occurs usually on the penultimate or final syllable ..." p.156: "... with stress on the final syllable. More study is needed to define the rules of such stress. (727) to-'hra 'not going' (728) …

sources.quote: 22.5 Word stress. The word stress on two-syllable words in Wai Wai normally occurs on the last syllable of the word. ... nouns or adverbs having three syllables and having a CV pattern stress normally occurs on the last syllable. If they have four syllables, the stress falls on the penultimate syllable. In either case stress falls on the syllable following the syllable having the long vowel.

sources.quote: p.9-10: 'A intensidade, ou tonicidade, é indicada pelo acento agudo ... a presença ou a ausência da tonicidade num morfema dado depende da sua posição no vocábulo inteiro. Em uaiuai a grande maioria dos vocábulos que recebem o acento são oxítonos, encontrando-se alguns paroxítonos. A tonicidade não cai antes da penúltima sílaba do vocábulo, exceto em caso de elisão. Alguns sufixos, porém, admitem a tonicidade só quando esta indica ênfase especial. Nos demais casos o acento intensivo cai na sílaba anterior ao referido sufixo, quando êste termina o vocábulo, e numa sílaba depois do dito sufixo,

sources.note: The database codes Waiwai with 14 consonants, 6 vowels /i ɨ u e o a/ and 'Suprasegmental: None', i.e. no tone and no suprasegmental nasal feature recorded, on the basis of Hawkins 1998 and Derbyshire 1999. A secondhand no-tone coding, not a description; it agrees with the absence of any lexical-tone mention in Hawkins 1998 (whose only uses of 'tone' are for sentence intonation) and in Acácio 2011.
